content: 1. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of applying chlorhexidine to the umbilical cord stump in newborns compared to dry cord care or usual cord care practices. The review aimed to determine whether this intervention reduces neonatal mortality rates, systemic sepsis, or omphalitis during the neonatal period. 2. Five trials involving approximately 56,600 neonates were included in the review. These trials examined the effects of single or multiple applications of chlorhexidine and reported critical outcomes such as neonatal mortality rate (NMR), omphalitis, and time to cord separation. However, none of the studies reported the incidence of neonatal sepsis. 3. Regarding neonatal mortality, data from three cluster-randomized controlled trials (CRCTs) conducted in South Asia, where home births and high neonatal mortality rates are common, showed a significant but moderate-sized benefit of chlorhexidine application. The quality of evidence was graded as low. 4. Four studies reported the incidence of omphalitis, defined as redness extending to the skin with or without pus, following chlorhexidine application. The pooled effect demonstrated a 30% reduction in omphalitis rates (95% CI: 20% to 38%). The quality of evidence was graded as moderate. 5. The application of chlorhexidine to the umbilical cord was associated with a longer time to cord separation. No data were available on other potential shortor long-term adverse effects. 6. The observed benefits of chlorhexidine application were primarily derived from studies conducted in high-mortality settings with predominantly home births (>90%) in South Asia. These findings may not be generalizable to settings where most births occur in health facilities and neonatal mortality rates are lower. Ongoing studies are investigating the intervention's effects in African settings. 7. Health providers and policymakers in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) with high neonatal mortality rates are likely to value the observed reduction in NMR and omphalitis. However, concerns about interference with essential newborn care practices, such as skin-to-skin care and early breastfeeding initiation, may arise if chlorhexidine is applied within the first hour after birth. 8. Chlorhexidine solution is inexpensive and can be made available even in resource-restricted settings. 9. Delayed bathing of newborns is recommended until at least 24 hours after birth. If cultural reasons prevent this, bathing should be delayed for at least six hours. Appropriate clothing for ambient temperature, including one to two layers more than adults and the use of hats or caps, is advised. 10. Mothers and newborns should not be separated and should remain in the same room 24 hours a day. Communication and play with the newborn should be encouraged. 11. Preterm and low-birth-weight babies should be identified immediately after birth and provided with special care according to existing WHO guidelines. 12. Postpartum women should undergo regular assessments of vaginal bleeding, uterine contraction, fundal height, temperature, and heart rate during the first 24 hours after birth. Blood pressure should be measured shortly after birth and again within six hours if normal. Urine voiding should be documented within six hours. 13. Beyond 24 hours, postnatal assessments should include inquiries about general well-being, urinary and bowel function, perineal wound healing, headache, fatigue, back pain, perineal pain and hygiene, breast pain, uterine tenderness, and lochia. Breastfeeding progress should also be evaluated. 14. Women should be asked about their emotional well-being, family and social support, and coping strategies for daily matters. Any changes in mood, emotional state, or behavior outside the woman's normal pattern should be reported to healthcare professionals. 15. At 10–14 days postpartum, women should be asked about the resolution of mild, transient postpartum depression (maternal blues). If symptoms persist, further assessment for postnatal depression should be conducted. 16. Women should be observed for signs of domestic abuse and informed about who to contact for advice and management. They should also be asked about resumption of sexual intercourse and possible dyspareunia as part of overall well-being assessment two to six weeks after birth. 17. Women should receive counseling on the physiological recovery process after birth, common health problems, and when to report health concerns. Specific signs and symptoms to report include postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, infection, and thromboembolism. 18. Counseling on nutrition, hygiene (especially handwashing), birth spacing, family planning, and safer sex practices, including condom use, should be provided. In malaria-endemic areas, mothers and babies should sleep under insecticide-impregnated bed nets. 19. Women should be encouraged to mobilize as soon as appropriate after birth, engage in gentle exercise, and take time to rest during the postnatal period. 20. Iron and folic acid supplementation should be provided for at least three months after delivery to prevent postpartum anemia. Although evidence is limited, the potential benefits of supplementation in reducing anemia-related health burdens outweigh the risks of major harmful side effects. 21. Prophylactic antibiotics are recommended for women with thirdor fourth-degree perineal tears following vaginal delivery to prevent wound complications. However, there is insufficient evidence to recommend routine antibiotic use for all low-risk women after vaginal delivery to prevent endometritis. 22. The lack of evidence for postnatal assessments and interventions highlights the need for urgent high-quality research in this area. However, clear recommendations for routine postnatal care are essential for setting quality standards. 23. Nutritional supplements, while relatively inexpensive, require adequately trained and equipped health workers for effective implementation.
